newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan advises India to shun "negative" acts.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan advises India to shun "negative" acts.

text.p: Pakistani government leaders advised India on Saturday to avoid taking what they called negative steps so that current peace talks between the two arch-rival neighbours could succeed.

Both President Farooq Leghari and Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif gave the advice to India's top foreign ministry official Salman Haider when he made courtesy calls on them on Friday, according to Pakistani official statements about the meetings.
Haider was later due to meet his Pakistani counterpart Shamshad Ahmad for the second session of the second round of dialogue the two sides launched in March.

Among what Pakistan calls "negative factors" Leghari and Sharif cited a recent alleged violation of Pakistani air space by an Indian spy plane, alleged deployment of missiles near the border and a border clash in which a Pakistan army officer was killed. India denies the air violation and missile deployment.

The official statement quoted Sharif as calling for a reduction of India's forces in the Indian-ruled part of the disputed Himalayan region of Jammu and Kashmir and improvement of human rights situation there.
"The progress should be uniform on a broad spectrum of Indo-Pakistan issues, including the core issue of Kashmir," Sharif said about the current moves by the two countries to improve their relations.
Sharif, raising the issue of air space violation and deployment of missiles, said: "All these negative factors should be avoided so as not to delay or complicate the prospects of dialogue."

Leghari also said such events should be avoided in order to maintain a conducive atmosphere for the dialogue between the two countries, which have fought three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947.

Haider told Sharif that Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral had asked him to assure Islamabad Delhi "wanted to open a new chapter in the relations between the two countries", according to the Pakistani statement.
Both sides said on Friday after the first session of talks that they hoped to devise a mechanism for future meetings.

Apart from an agreement to pursue the dialogue, little emerged from the first round of talks in Delhi in March, but they paved the way for the two foreign ministers to meet in April and the two prime ministers to get together in May.
The Delhi meeting of foreign secretaries resumed a dialogue which foundered in 1994 over the issue of Kashmir, two-thirds of which is ruled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
